267.title: The shortest great sutra
267.hook: a few lines on the perfection of wisdom, chanted daily across East Asia and Tibet; read in Müller's 1894 translation
267.howItsDone: The Heart Sutra is chanted daily in many Zen, Chan, Korean Seon and Tibetan communities, often at morning and evening services; Theravada communities do not use it as scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your four foundations. Your line was four places to stand: body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Did you find the body first when you felt lost? Day two hundred sixty-seven, and a new part of the path.
screen: `YOUR FOUR FOUNDATIONS — FOUR PLACES TO STAND.`

segments.voice: Walk into a Zen temple in Kyoto early in the morning, or a Korean mountain monastery, or a Tibetan prayer hall, and there's a good chance you'll hear the same short text being chanted. In Chinese it's only around two hundred sixty characters. It fits on a single page. People print it on fans, scrolls, and tea cups. Monks know it by heart; so do many grandmothers. For the next ten days, we'll read it slowly, line by line. Today's word: prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom.
screen: `A ZEN TEMPLE, A MOUNTAIN MONASTERY.` → `ONE PAGE, CHANTED EVERYWHERE.` → `TEN DAYS, LINE BY LINE.`

segments.voice: Its full name is the Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, usually just called the Heart Sutra. It belongs to the Mahayana, the branch of Buddhism found across East Asia, Tibet, Mongolia and Vietnam. Theravada Buddhists, who have walked with us through the Pali texts these past weeks, don't use it as scripture; it comes from a different family of texts, and both families are honored by their own communities. Prajnaparamita is two Sanskrit words. Prajna is wisdom, the deep seeing that understands how things really are. Paramita is perfection, but there's a famous traditional reading of it: para, the far shore, and ita, gone. Wisdom gone beyond. Wisdom that has crossed over. Scholars today think the word more likely comes from parama, the highest. But the image of crossing has stuck for centuries, and the text itself will use it. There's a whole library of perfection-of-wisdom texts, some of them enormous, one version running to a hundred thousand lines. The Heart Sutra is their heart: the whole teaching pressed into a page. There's also an English connection. In the eighteen eighties, Max Müller in Oxford, working with the Japanese scholar Bunyiu Nanjio, published the Sanskrit text from old palm leaves kept at the temple of Horyuji in Japan. Müller's English translation appeared in eighteen ninety-four. So it's a short text, with a very long reach.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE PERFECTION OF WISDOM.` · `A MAHAYANA TEXT.` · `PRAJNA + PARAMITA: WISDOM GONE BEYOND.` · `PALM LEAVES AT HORYUJI.` · then, large: `WISDOM GONE BEYOND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For now, let the sit be simple: rest with the breath, and hold one phrase lightly, wisdom gone beyond. Picture a river, and the far shore. Don't try to cross. Just know the shore is there. Later today, if you'd like, find a copy of the Heart Sutra, Müller's translation is freely available, and read it once, slowly, out loud if you can. Don't try to understand it yet. The bell holds the time.
Prajnaparamita. The perfection of wisdom, or, in the old reading, wisdom gone beyond: the heart of a whole library, pressed into one page.
Your line: wisdom gone beyond. Today, read the Heart Sutra once, slowly, in any translation you have, and notice one line that catches you. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

no, it's forbidden.

268.title: Avalokiteshvara looks deep
268.hook: the bodhisattva of compassion, practicing deep wisdom, sees the five heaps empty
268.howItsDone: Devotion to Avalokiteshvara, as Guanyin, Kannon, Gwaneum or Chenrezig, is among the most widespread in Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhism; many practitioners chant the Heart Sutra, which opens with this bodhisattva, alongside mantras and prayers to Avalokiteshvara.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prajnaparamita, and your line was wisdom gone beyond. Did you read the Heart Sutra once? Which line caught you? Day two hundred sixty-eight.

If you've ever seen a statue of a serene figure with a thousand arms, each hand holding out something different, or a graceful white-robed figure in a Chinese garden, or a small shrine in a Japanese hospital, you may have met the same being under different names. In China she's often Guanyin. In Japan, Kannon. In Tibet, Chenrezig. In India, where the name began, Avalokiteshvara. And the Heart Sutra opens by pointing straight at this figure. Today's word: Avalokiteshvara.
screen: `A THOUSAND ARMS, A WHITE ROBE.` → `GUANYIN, KANNON, CHENREZIG.` → `WHERE THE HEART SUTRA BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In the Mahayana, a bodhisattva is someone on the way to full awakening who vows to help all beings get there too. Avalokiteshvara is the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears the cries of the world. The name is usually read as avalokita, looking down or looking upon, and ishvara, lord: the lord who looks down with compassion. In the art, the thousand arms are for reaching everyone who calls. In Tibet, the Dalai Lamas are regarded as his emanations. In East Asia, over the centuries, the figure came to be shown most often as female. Here's what's surprising about the Heart Sutra's first line. It doesn't show Avalokiteshvara doing something compassionate. It shows the bodhisattva looking. Practicing deep in the perfection of wisdom, the text says, Avalokiteshvara looked closely and saw five heaps, and saw that they were empty. Five heaps: you met them a week ago, the khandhas. Form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. The Pali name was khandha; here, in Sanskrit, it's skandha. Same five. What it means for them to be empty is where the sutra goes next, and we'll take it slowly tomorrow. For today, notice the pairing. The being most famous for compassion is the one who teaches wisdom. In Mahayana teaching the two are often called the two wings of a bird: compassion without wisdom can't see clearly, and wisdom without compassion doesn't fly. The sutra begins with both in one figure.
screen: `THE ONE WHO HEARS THE WORLD'S CRIES.` · `THE LORD WHO LOOKS DOWN.` · `LOOKING DEEP AT THE FIVE HEAPS.` · `COMPASSION AND WISDOM: TWO WINGS.` · then, large: `LOOK DEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Choose one thing near you: your own hand, a leaf, a pen. Look at it deeply, the way Avalokiteshvara looks. Not a quick glance: stay with it. Notice its color, its edges, its texture, and then the feeling tone it brings, pleasant, unpleasant or neither, and the label your mind puts on it. Look as if you'd never seen one before. Then close your eyes and rest. The bell holds the time.
Avalokiteshvara. The bodhisattva of compassion, the lord who looks down, who in the Heart Sutra looks deep and sees the five heaps empty.
Your line: look deep. Today, choose one ordinary thing, or one ordinary person, and look at them twice as long as usual, with care. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

269.title: Form is emptiness
269.hook: form is emptiness, emptiness is form: nothing stands on its own
269.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists chant 'form is emptiness, emptiness is form' daily as part of the Heart Sutra, and many teachers explain emptiness through dependent arising: nothing exists on its own, apart from causes and conditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who looks deep. Your line was look deep. What did you look at twice as long as usual? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

Pick up the nearest cup. Now ask: where did it come from? A store, fine. Before that, a factory, or a potter's wheel. Before that, clay dug from a riverbank, water, a kiln's fire, fuel for the fire, the trucks, the roads, the people who made the roads, and the breakfasts that fed them. The longer you follow the threads, the more the cup seems less like one solid thing and more like a knot where a thousand threads cross. That's a way in to the most famous line in the Heart Sutra. Today's word: shunyata, emptiness.
screen: `WHERE DID THE CUP COME FROM?` → `CLAY, WATER, FIRE, ROADS, BREAKFASTS.` → `A KNOT OF A THOUSAND THREADS.`

segments.voice: Right after Avalokiteshvara sees the five heaps empty, the sutra turns to the monk Shariputra and says the line people chant across Asia: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. Emptiness is not different from form, and form is not different from emptiness. Then the same is said for feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Shunyata comes from shunya, empty. It's the same Sanskrit word Indian mathematicians used for zero. But in Mahayana teaching, empty always means empty of something. And what things are empty of is svabhava, own-being: an existence that stands on its own, from its own side, depending on nothing else. So form is emptiness means: the cup, the body, any form at all, has no being that stands alone. It is made entirely of other things, causes and conditions, clay and fire and hands. And emptiness is form means: this emptiness isn't somewhere else, in some other realm. It's right here as the cup. It's what the cup is like. You might hear an echo. In the Pali texts you've been reading, the Buddha taught dependent arising, that everything comes to be because of other things. Mahayana teachers, and especially the second-century philosopher Nagarjuna, drew that thread all the way out: if everything depends on other things, then nothing has a self of its own. That's emptiness. It isn't gloomy. Many Buddhists find it the opposite: nothing stands alone, so nothing is truly alone.
screen: `FORM IS EMPTINESS, EMPTINESS IS FORM.` · `SHUNYA: EMPTY, THE SAME WORD AS ZERO.` · `EMPTY OF OWN-BEING.` · `EVERYTHING DEPENDS ON OTHER THINGS.` · then, large: `NOTHING STANDS ALONE.`

segments.voice: Hold a cup, or picture one. Trace what it depends on: the material, the maker, the fire, the water, the hands that carried it, the sun that grew the food for those hands. Follow three or four threads as far as they go. Then look at the cup again. It's still a cup. And it's also a meeting place of countless things. Let both be true at once. The bell holds the time.
Shunyata. Emptiness: not nothing, but empty of standing alone. Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
Your line: nothing stands alone. Today, pick one thing you use, a phone, a shirt, a meal, and name five things it depends on. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

fork.setup: you're Shariputra, and you've just heard 'form is emptiness.' what comes right after?

'and emptiness is form: not different from each other.'

fork.reveal: the sutra balances it at once: emptiness is form. emptiness isn't somewhere else; it's how form is.

what it means: nothing stands on its own; everything is made of other things.

270.title: Emptiness is not nothing
270.hook: Mahayana teachers stress it: empty of a separate self, not non-existent; the cup still holds tea
270.howItsDone: Mahayana teachers regularly caution students against reading emptiness as nihilism, and in many East Asian traditions a mindful cup of tea is used as a small, everyday practice of seeing things as empty and interdependent.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shunyata, emptiness, and your line was nothing stands alone. What five things did your one thing depend on? Day two hundred seventy.

Tell a friend that the Buddhists say everything is empty, and watch their face. Some hear it as bleak: so nothing matters? Others hear it as a trick: so I don't really exist, and neither does my rent? Some even hear it as a free pass: if it's all empty, why be kind? Every one of those reactions is a misunderstanding the Buddhist tradition saw coming, a very long time ago. Its teachers went out of their way to warn against it. Today: emptiness is not nothing.
screen: `'SO NOTHING MATTERS?'` → `'SO MY RENT ISN'T REAL?'` → `A MISUNDERSTANDING SEEN COMING.`

segments.voice: Go back to the cup from yesterday. It's empty of standing alone: made of clay, fire, water, hands. But pour tea into it, and it holds the tea. It doesn't leak because it's empty of own-being. It works because it's made of all those things. That's the point Mahayana teachers keep making. Empty doesn't mean non-existent. It means dependent. The cup is real as a cup that depends on causes; it just isn't real as a cup that stands on its own. The philosopher Nagarjuna, whose writing on emptiness shaped much of the Mahayana, also warned about getting it wrong. Misunderstood emptiness, he wrote, ruins the person of weak understanding, like a snake grabbed the wrong way. You may remember the kusa grass in the Dhammapada, cutting the hand that grasps it badly. It's the same warning in a new place. Grab emptiness by the edge, and it turns into nothing matters. Grab it rightly, and it turns into everything is connected. And here's the part that surprises people. In Mahayana teaching, understanding emptiness is supposed to make compassion stronger, not weaker. If nothing stands alone, then my well-being and yours aren't separate. Teachers often point out that the Heart Sutra is spoken by Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Emptiness and caring aren't opposites. Teachers often describe it this way: empty of a separate self, and full of everything else. The cup is empty, and the cup is full.
screen: `THE CUP STILL HOLDS TEA.` · `EMPTY MEANS DEPENDENT, NOT NON-EXISTENT.` · `A SNAKE GRABBED THE WRONG WAY.` · `EMPTINESS MAKES COMPASSION STRONGER.` · then, large: `EMPTY AND FULL.`

segments.voice: If you have a warm drink nearby, hold it. If not, picture one. Feel the warmth. Then, sip by sip, or breath by breath, name what's in it: water from somewhere, leaves grown by someone, heat from somewhere else, the cup, your own hands. Empty of standing alone. And still here, still warm, still good to drink. Empty and full at once. The bell holds the time.
Emptiness is not nothing. Empty of a separate self, not empty of existence: the cup still holds the tea.
Your line: empty and full. Today, with one cup of tea or coffee or water, drink it slowly and remember its causes, and that it still quenches your thirst. Day two hundred seventy.

it's meant to strengthen it: if nothing stands alone, no one's well-being is separate.

'don't think about emptiness at all.'
fork.reveal: Mahayana teachers treat emptiness and compassion as partners. the Heart Sutra is even spoken by the bodhisattva of compassion.

original.note: Sanskrit svabhāva: own-being, what things are empty of; not existence itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: emptiness is a fancy word for nothingness.
what it means: empty of standing alone, full of causes and connections.

sources.work: Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way

271.title: Not born, not destroyed
271.hook: all things marked by emptiness: not born, not destroyed, not stained, not pure, not growing, not shrinking
271.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia, Tibet and beyond chant the Heart Sutra's line about things being not born and not destroyed in daily services and at funerals, where teachers often explain it through the two truths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: emptiness is not nothing, and your line, empty and full. Did a cup of tea turn out to hold the rain, the field and the hands that picked it? Day two hundred seventy-one.
screen: `EMPTINESS IS NOT NOTHING — EMPTY AND FULL.`

segments.voice: Drop an ice cube into a glass of water and watch it. The edges soften. It shrinks. A minute later there's no ice cube. So when did it die? And where did it go? Nothing left the glass. The water is a little colder and a little fuller. The cube didn't vanish into nothing, and it didn't come from nothing either: it was water before the freezer got to it. We still say, the ice is gone. That's true, and it's useful. But it isn't the whole story. Today the Heart Sutra says something that sounds impossible, about everything.
screen: `AN ICE CUBE IN A GLASS.` → `WHEN DID IT DIE?` → `NOTHING LEFT THE GLASS.`

segments.voice: Avalokiteshvara is still speaking to Shariputra. Having said form is emptiness, he goes on: all things are marked by emptiness. They are not born and not destroyed. Not stained and not pure. Not growing and not shrinking. Three pairs, six nots. In Sanskrit the first two are anutpanna, not arisen, and aniruddha, not ceased. Here's the thread. Two days ago you heard that nothing stands alone: everything is made of causes and conditions. If that's true, nothing starts from zero. A tree was a seed, and the seed was a tree, and both were rain and soil and sun. And nothing ends at zero. When the tree falls, it becomes soil for the next one. Birth and death are real names for real changes, but they're names for a shift in conditions, not for something popping in or out of existence. The same with stained and pure. Dirt isn't a fixed essence stuck to a thing, and neither is cleanness. Mahayana teachers explain this with two truths. At the everyday level, people are born, people die, and grief is honest. At the deepest level, they say, nothing has a separate self that could be born or destroyed. Both levels are true at once, and the teachers never tell a grieving person that the loss isn't real. The sutra itself doesn't explain any of this. It's famous for being short. The explanations come from commentators in India, China and Tibet, and they don't all agree on the details. What they share is the direction: look closely at an ending, and you find a change.
screen: `THREE PAIRS, SIX NOTS.` · `NOTHING STARTS FROM ZERO.` · `NOTHING ENDS AT ZERO.` · `TWO TRUTHS AT ONCE.` · then, large: `NO BIRTH, NO DEATH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath come in on its own. Notice where this breath was a moment ago: outside you, part of the room. Now it's inside, warm. Then it goes back out and becomes the room again. When did it begin? When does it end? You don't need an answer. Just watch the air change places. If a thought appears, notice that it too came from somewhere, and goes somewhere. Rest in the coming and going. The bell holds the time.
Not born. Anutpanna, not arisen: in the Heart Sutra, things marked by emptiness don't start from nothing or end in nothing. They change.
Your line: no birth, no death. Today, when something ends, a meal, a day, a song, ask what it became. Day two hundred seventy-one.

match.prompt: match each pair in the Heart Sutra's line.

the sutra lists three pairs of 'nots'
not born, not destroyed; not stained, not pure; not growing, not shrinking.
Mahayana teachers use two truths to explain the line
everyday birth and death are real; at the deepest level nothing has a separate self to be born.

fork.setup: a friend whose grandmother just died has heard the Heart Sutra line. she asks you: so it's saying she didn't really die? what do today's teachers say?
options: yes, so there's nothing to grieve.
her death is real at the everyday level; the line points at what she was made of and passed on.

fork.reveal: Mahayana teachers hold two truths at once: the loss is real and grief is honest, and at the deepest level nothing had a separate self that could vanish into nothing.

original.note: Sanskrit anutpanna: not arisen, unborn; the Heart Sutra pairs it with aniruddha, not ceased.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'not born, not destroyed' means nothing really happens.
what it means: nothing starts from zero or ends at zero; birth and death name changes in conditions.
what a scholar hears: the pair echoes Nagarjuna's opening verses, which list eight negations beginning 'no ceasing, no arising', and the two-truths teaching comes from the same Madhyamaka school.

sources.work: Nagarjuna, Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way

272.title: No eye, no ear
272.hook: in emptiness no eye, no ear, even no four truths as fixed things: the list itself held lightly
272.howItsDone: In Zen and other Mahayana communities the long run of 'no' lines is chanted briskly as part of the daily Heart Sutra, while the same lists (the five heaps, the four truths) are still taught in study and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not born, and your line, no birth, no death. Did something end, a meal or a song, and did you ask what it became? Day two hundred seventy-two.

Think of the most useful list you own. A grocery list. A packing list for a trip. A checklist a pilot runs before takeoff. Lists are wonderful. They carry what your memory can't. But you've probably met someone who holds a list too tightly. The trip where the plan mattered more than the people. The recipe followed so exactly that nobody noticed the soup was too salty. Buddhism is full of lists: four truths, five heaps, eight steps on the path, twelve links. Today the Heart Sutra does something startling. It picks up Buddhism's own lists, one by one, and says no.
screen: `A GROCERY LIST. A PILOT'S CHECKLIST.` → `HELD TOO TIGHTLY.` → `BUDDHISM'S OWN LISTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the passage, in plain words. In emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, no consciousness. That's the five heaps, the list of what a person is made of. No eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind. No sights, no sounds, no smells, all the way through. That's the list of the senses and their objects. No ignorance and no end of ignorance, all the way to no old age and death and no end of old age and death. That's the twelve links of dependent arising. And then: no suffering, no cause of suffering, no ending, no path. The four noble truths themselves. No wisdom and no attaining. Why would a Buddhist text say no to the four truths? Not to throw them away. Mahayana Buddhists still teach every one of those lists. The no means: none of these is a fixed thing standing on its own. Each is a way of seeing, a tool. Some scholars read the passage as a gentle pushback on earlier schools that had catalogued the building blocks of experience in great detail and treated them as the bedrock of reality. There's an older picture for the same idea, in a sutta the Theravada tradition also keeps. The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft. You build it to cross a river. Once across, you don't carry it on your head through the forest. The raft was real, and it worked. Holding it lightly is how you keep walking.
screen: `NO FORM, NO FEELING.` · `NO EYE, NO EAR.` · `NO SUFFERING, NO PATH.` · `THE RAFT ACROSS THE RIVER.` · then, large: `HOLD LISTS LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Pick one list you carry: today's to-dos, a list of rules for yourself, a list of what's wrong. Hold it in mind for a breath. Now set it down beside you, like a raft on the riverbank. It's still there. You can pick it up later. Then just listen. When a sound comes, you might notice the label forming, car, voice, fridge. Let the label go and stay with the hearing itself. The bell holds the time.
No eye. In emptiness, the Heart Sutra says, even the senses and the four truths aren't fixed things. The lists are tools.
Your line: hold lists lightly. Today, when a plan or a checklist starts to matter more than the person in front of you, loosen your grip by one finger. Day two hundred seventy-two.

match.prompt: match each 'no' to the list it comes from.

myth: the Heart Sutra tells Buddhists to throw out the four noble truths
Mahayana Buddhists still teach them; the 'no' says they aren't fixed things standing alone.
the sutra also says 'no wisdom and no attaining'
it doesn't exempt even wisdom from the list.
the raft picture comes from a sutta the Theravada tradition keeps
the Buddha compares his teaching to a raft for crossing, not for carrying on your head.

fork.setup: you've crossed a river on a raft you built yourself. it was hard work and it held. what does the Buddha's picture suggest you do now?
options: carry it on your head, in case.
burn it, since it was never real.
leave it on the bank and keep walking.
fork.reveal: the raft worked and was real; the point is not to carry it once it has done its job.

original.note: Sanskrit 'na cakṣuḥ': no eye. The Heart Sutra runs through eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'no eye, no ear' means the sutra denies you can see or hear.
what it means: even Buddhism's own lists, senses and truths included, are tools, not fixed things.

what a scholar hears: the passage walks through the classic Abhidharma categories (five aggregates, twelve sense bases, eighteen elements, twelve links, four truths) and negates each as ultimately real.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita-hrdaya), 'in emptiness there is no form…'

273.title: Nothing to attain
273.hook: because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva rests in wisdom
273.howItsDone: Zen communities, especially in the Soto school, often describe sitting meditation as practice without gaining ideas, and the Heart Sutra's 'nothing to attain' is chanted daily in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no eye, and your line, hold lists lightly. Did a plan loosen its grip by one finger? Day two hundred seventy-three, the end of the week.

Almost everything in a modern day is built around getting somewhere. Step counts. Inbox zero. The next level, the next degree, the next promotion. Even this app counts days, and you're on day two hundred seventy-three. Goals are good. They get people out of bed. But notice what happens inside when the goal becomes the whole point: the present turns into a hallway you're rushing through on the way to the real room. Today the Heart Sutra says something that sounds like it would put every self-improvement book out of business. There is nothing to attain.
screen: `STEP COUNTS. INBOX ZERO.` → `THE PRESENT AS A HALLWAY.` → `NOTHING TO ATTAIN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's long run of no's ended with: no wisdom and no attaining. Then the sutra draws the conclusion. Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva relies on the perfection of wisdom. The Sanskrit is aprāptitva: the state of not-getting. It's a strange thing to find in a text about awakening. Isn't awakening the goal? Here's how Mahayana teachers answer. If awakening were an object, something you could get, then you could also grab at it, hoard it, compare yours with someone else's. That grabbing is the very craving the path is meant to loosen. So the sutra says: it isn't a thing you add to yourself. It's seeing clearly what was already here. In Japan, the Zen teacher Dogen put it in his own way: sitting isn't a means to awakening later; sitting is awakening, expressed now. Notice what the sutra does not say. It doesn't say stop practicing. The bodhisattva still relies on wisdom, still works for the good of all beings. The effort stays. What drops is the grabbing. Look back at the week. You met the shortest great sutra and its name, wisdom gone beyond. Avalokiteshvara looked deep. Form is emptiness, and nothing stands alone. Emptiness is not nothing: empty and full. Not born: no birth, no death. No eye: hold lists lightly. And now the end of the list. Nothing to get.
screen: `APRĀPTITVA: NOT-GETTING.` · `AWAKENING IS NOT AN OBJECT.` · `THE EFFORT STAYS, THE GRABBING GOES.` · `A WEEK OF THE HEART SUTRA.` · then, large: `NOTHING TO GET.`

segments.voice: For this sit, try having no goal. Not a calm mind, not a good session, not even a better breath. Sit comfortably and let whatever happens happen. If you catch yourself trying to do it well, smile at that, and let the trying go too. If the mind wanders, that's what's happening, so that's the practice. There's nowhere this sit needs to get to. You're already here. The bell holds the time.
Nothing to attain. Because awakening isn't a thing to grab, the Heart Sutra says, the bodhisattva rests in wisdom instead of reaching.
Your line: nothing to get. Today, pick one thing you'd usually rush through toward a result, a walk, a chore, a conversation, and do it for its own sake. Day two hundred seventy-three.

match.prompt: match each piece of this week's Heart Sutra.

myth: 'nothing to attain' means Buddhists should stop practicing
the bodhisattva still relies on wisdom and works for others; what drops is the grabbing.
the line comes right after 'no wisdom and no attaining'
the sutra draws its conclusion from that list.
Dogen taught that sitting is only a means to awakening later
he taught that sitting is awakening, expressed now.

fork.setup: you've been meditating for months and a friend asks: so, have you got it yet? what would the Heart Sutra point to?
options: not yet, but I'm close.
awakening isn't an object to get; the practice goes on without grabbing.
yes, and it's better than yours.
fork.reveal: the sutra says there is nothing to attain, so the bodhisattva rests in wisdom rather than chasing a prize.

original.note: Sanskrit aprāptitva: the state of not-attaining; the Heart Sutra's reason the bodhisattva relies on the perfection of wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'nothing to attain' means the path is pointless.
what it means: awakening isn't an object to grab; the effort stays and the grabbing drops.
what a scholar hears: aprāptitva answers the Abhidharma term prāpti ('possession'), a force one school said links a person to their attainments; the sutra denies even that.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita-hrdaya), 'because there is nothing to attain…'
Dogen, Shobogenzo, 'Bendowa' (practice and realization are one)
